chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Abu al-Jawza', from al-Husayn ibn 'Ulwān, from Zayd ibn 'Alī, from his fathers, from 'Alī (peace be upon him) who said:

A man came to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, my father freed a slave belonging to me, to my detriment.' The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'You and your wealth are a gift of Allah to your father; you are a share from his quiver. He gives to whom he wishes females, and he gives to whom he wishes males, and he makes whom he wishes barren.' The manumission of your father is valid; your father takes from your wealth and your body, and you do not take from his wealth or his body anything except by his permission.'

key_terms.بَدَنٌ: Body/self (referring to the person's own self or capacity)

ai.seo_question: What is the legal ruling when a father frees a slave owned by his son?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the juristic principle of *al-abu min waladihi ka-al-nis'a fi al-mal* (the father is like a female heir to his son's property), illustrating that a father's manumission of a son's slave is valid because he holds a proprietary share in the son's wealth and body. The narration highlights the asymmetry in rights: while the father can unilaterally dispose of the son's assets, the son cannot reclaim them without the father's consent, a concept rooted in the patriarchal structure of early Islamic inheritance and guardianship. This ruling is frequently cited by Shia jurists to discuss the extent of paternal authority over minor or adult sons' property in the absence of explicit legal barriers.
